## Overview

**Job Market Analysis** — part of the [Data Science Projects Collection](https://github.com/PaulChanCyber/Data-Science-Project-). Salary prediction and skill-demand analysis from Cambodian job postings (ITC PDS 2022–2023).

## Background of the Study

This study examines **Cambodian online job boards and salary listings** in Cambodia—a context where digital classifieds and e-commerce listings have accelerated price transparency but not necessarily price *understanding*. Stakeholders include job seekers, career centers, and hiring managers. **Job Analysis Report: Salary Prediction** — ITC PDS 2022–2023. Team: SENG Lay, VANNAK Vireakyuth, YA Manon, VANN Visal, TAING Kimmeng, VINLAY Anusar. Instructor **CHAN Sophal**. The project folder on GitHub contains notebooks, and in many cases a formal **Project Guideline** PDF that records the instructor-approved objectives, timeline, and evaluation plan. That document is the contract between the student team and the course: it states what will be delivered, which algorithms will be compared, and how success will be measured. The work was completed in the **Programming for Data Science (PDS)** course at the **Institute of Technology of Cambodia (ITC)**, Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, under instructor **CHAN Sophal**. Deliverables typically include a **Project Guideline** alignment document, Jupyter notebooks, visualizations, a written report, and presentation slides—mirroring how data analysts are expected to document real engagements for technical and non-technical audiences.

## Motivation of the Study

**Why this topic matters:** Knowing which skills correlate with higher pay guides training investments and hiring strategy. Students and job seekers in Cambodia need evidence on which skills and roles command higher salaries in local postings. From an academic standpoint, **Job Market Analysis** trains competencies employers list repeatedly: pandas data wrangling, visualization literacy, scikit-learn modeling, and clear written communication. From a practical standpoint, even a simple benchmark model helps job seekers, career centers, and hiring managers negotiate fairer deals and spot overpriced listings. The motivation is therefore both **social** (fairer, more informed transactions) and **pedagogical** (evidence that the team followed the guideline, compared models fairly, and can explain limitations such as sample bias, missing data, and temporal drift).

## Project Guidelines & Objectives

The following objectives and steps are taken from the team's **Project Guideline** (see GitHub) and reflect how the instructor graded the capstone: **From *Guideline* (Job Analysis):**

- **Introduction** to salary prediction study
- **Problem statement:** objectives, constraints, **expected deliverables**, **success criteria**
- **Data collection & preprocessing:** scrape job boards; text preprocessing; feature extraction/encoding; train/test split; imbalance handling if needed
- **EDA:** descriptive stats, visualizations
- **Modeling** for salary prediction (see full report in repo) Teams were expected to show intermediate artifacts—not only a final accuracy number. That includes data dictionaries, plots defending modeling choices, and a short conclusion on which model to deploy or recommend for the stated business question.

## Data Collection & Preparation

Reliable conclusions depend on documenting **where data came from**, **how often it was collected**, and **what each column means**. For this project: Scraped Cambodian job postings with role, skills, experience, and salary fields where available. Typical preparation steps across PDS scraping projects include deduplicating listings, standardizing currencies (USD vs. KHR), parsing text fields (e.g., '3+ bedrooms'), handling missing values with explicit rules, and flagging extreme prices before modeling. Those steps reduce leakage and prevent a single erroneous row from dominating metrics.

## Methodology & Analysis

Analytical work proceeded in reproducible notebook stages so instructors could rerun cells during defense sessions: NLP-style text preprocessing on titles/descriptions; categorical encoding; regression or classification toward salary bands. Where applicable, teams compared multiple algorithms rather than reporting a single default model. Feature engineering was justified with plots (distributions, correlations, geographic breakdowns) so stakeholders could see *why* variables entered the model—not only *that* they improved error metrics.

## Model Evaluation

Model evaluation followed train/validation/test discipline taught in PDS: Success criteria from guideline—prediction error or tier accuracy vs. deliverables. Beyond scalar error, teams were encouraged to inspect **residuals** (regression), **confusion matrices** (classification), or **forecast overlays** (time series) to detect systematic bias—such as underpricing premium districts or overfitting rare categories.

## Results & Key Learnings

Skill-demand and salary insight report for career planning and curriculum alignment. Completing **Job Market Analysis** provides evidence of end-to-end data science execution: from raw scrape to defended conclusions. For portfolio readers, the GitHub repository contains the artifacts to verify claims—notebooks, and in many folders, slide decks and PDF reports. Limitations are worth stating explicitly: scraped data snapshots age quickly; models trained in 2022–2023 may need retraining as market conditions shift. That honesty is part of professional practice.
